lessons.title: The Nature of Allah and Core Muslim Beliefs
lessons.description: Tawhid, the Six Beliefs of Islam, the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din in Shi'a Islam, and the characteristics of Allah.
lessons.content_html:
The Foundation of Islamic Belief

Islam is built on a framework of core beliefs that shape everything a Muslim thinks, says and does. These beliefs differ slightly between the two main branches of Islam, Sunni and Shi’a. Both share fundamental convictions about Allah, but they organise and present those convictions in distinct frameworks that examiners expect you to know.

The split between Sunni and Shi’a Islam originates in a dispute over succession after the Prophet Muhammad’s death in 632 CE. The majority chose Abu Bakr as the first Caliph (successor), forming the Sunni tradition. A minority held that Muhammad had designated his cousin and son-in-law Ali ibn Abi Talib as his rightful heir, forming the Shi’a tradition. This dispute over authority produced two different but overlapping systems of belief.

The Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam

Sunni Muslims articulate their core beliefs through the Six Beliefs of Islam (also called the Six Articles of Faith). These come from the Qur’an and from the Kitab al-iman (Book of Faith), where the Prophet Muhammad described the pillars of belief. A hadith recorded in Kitab al-iman 1:4 records that faith requires belief in “Allah, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and al-Qadr.”

1. Tawhid — Oneness of Allah. The absolute, undivided unity of God. Surah 112 declares Allah is One, eternal and absolute, with no offspring and no equal.

2. Malaikah — Angels. Spiritual beings created from divine light who obey Allah perfectly, delivering revelation, recording deeds and carrying out His commands.

3. Kutub — Holy Books. Allah revealed scriptures to various prophets, including the Tawrat (Torah), the Zabur (Psalms), the Injil (Gospel) and, finally and completely, the Qur’an.

4. Risalah — Prophets. Allah sent prophets to every nation. Muhammad is the final prophet, the Seal of the Prophets, with no prophets to follow.

5. Yawm al-Din — Day of Judgement. At the end of time all people will be resurrected and judged by Allah on the basis of their beliefs and deeds.

6. Al-Qadr — Predestination. Allah has knowledge of all things, past, present and future. Everything that happens is within His knowledge and will.

Key Fact

The Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam — Allah, Angels, Books, Prophets, Day of Judgement, Predestination — are drawn from Kitab al-iman 1:4. This hadith text is the named source your exam expects you to cite for the Five Pillars of belief.

The Five Roots of Usul ad-Din (Shi’a Islam)

Shi’a Muslims organise core belief around the Usul ad-Din — the Five Roots or Principles of Religion. While the Six Beliefs and the Five Roots share much common ground, they differ in two significant ways: the Shi’a framework replaces al-Qadr (predestination) with Adl (Divine Justice), and adds Imamah (divinely guided leadership) as a distinctive pillar of faith.

1. Tawhid — The oneness of Allah. Shared with Sunni belief.

2. Adl (Adalat) — Divine Justice. Allah is perfectly just; He does not and cannot act unjustly. This is an active attribute: Allah’s justice is a guarantor of moral order. This replaces al-Qadr as a named Root because Shi’a scholars, concerned about predestination undermining human accountability, prefer to emphasise justice.

3. Nubuwwah — Prophethood. Allah sent messengers to guide humanity. Muhammad is the final prophet.

4. Imamah — Leadership. After Muhammad, the community should be led by a line of divinely appointed Imams from the family of the Prophet (Ahl-ul-Bayt). The Imam is believed to be sinless and divinely guided. Twelver Shi’a Muslims believe in twelve such Imams; Sevener (Ismaili) Shi’a follow the first seven.

5. Mi’ad — Resurrection and the Day of Judgement. All people will be raised and judged. Mi’ad is essentially equivalent to Yawm al-Din in Sunni belief.

Twelver Shi’a Muslims (Ithna’ashariyya) are the majority of Shi’a, dominant in Iran, Iraq and parts of Lebanon. They recognise twelve Imams, the last of whom (Muhammad al-Mahdi) is believed to have gone into divine occultation and will return at the end of time.

Sevener (Ismaili) Shi’a Muslims follow the first seven Imams. They accept Ismail ibn Jafar as the seventh Imam rather than his younger brother Musa al-Kazim, whom Twelvers follow. The Aga Khan is the current hereditary leader of the Nizari Ismaili community, the largest surviving Ismaili branch.

Tawhid — The Oneness of Allah

Tawhid is the single most important belief in Islam. It holds that Allah is absolutely One — undivided, unique, without partners, children or equals. Surah 112 (Al-Ikhlas) is the foundational Qur’anic text: it teaches that Allah is One, eternal and self-sufficient, was not born and has no offspring, and nothing is comparable to Him. Muslims recite this surah daily; it summarises the whole of Tawhid in four verses.

The opposite of Tawhid is Shirk (associating anything with Allah). Shirk is described in the Qur’an as the one sin Allah will not forgive if a person dies without repenting of it. This explains why Islamic art traditionally avoids depictions of Allah or the Prophet, using calligraphy and geometric patterns instead.

The Nature and Qualities of Allah

Muslims believe Allah possesses qualities revealed throughout the Qur’an. Key divine attributes include:

  • Omnipotence (all-powerful): Allah created the universe from nothing and sustains all life. Nothing is beyond His power.
  • Beneficence: Allah is supremely good and generous. His generosity extends to all creation.
  • Mercy (Ar-Rahman, Ar-Rahim): These two divine names both translate as “merciful” but are distinct. Ar-Rahman refers to Allah’s universal, boundless mercy that extends to all creation; Ar-Rahim refers to His particular and ongoing mercy towards believers. Every surah of the Qur’an (except one) opens with the phrase Bismillah ar-Rahman ar-Rahim (“In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful”).
  • Transcendence: Allah is beyond and above the physical world; He is not limited by time or space.
  • Immanence: At the same time, Allah is intimately close to His creation. The Qur’an states He is “closer to you than your jugular vein” (Surah 50:16).
Key Fact

Surah 16:35–36 is the Edexcel-named anchor for Allah’s oneness and prophethood: it declares that Allah sent a messenger to every nation, commanding: “Worship Allah and avoid false gods.” This verse links Tawhid to Risalah and underpins both the first and fourth articles of Sunni belief. In Shi’a Islam, Adalat (justice) is treated as a distinct Root of Religion, reflecting Shi’a theological emphasis on human moral accountability.

Comparing Muslim belief in Tawhid with Christian belief about the nature of God is a rich area for 12-mark Discuss answers.

  • Islam: God is absolutely one and indivisible. Any suggestion of a Trinity is rejected as Shirk. Allah has no son.
  • Christianity: God is one being in three persons — Father, Son and Holy Spirit (the Trinity). Christians affirm monotheism but understand God’s nature as Trinitarian. Catholics ground this in the Nicene Creed and the Catechism of the Catholic Church.
  • Judaism: Like Islam, Judaism insists on the absolute unity of God (the Shema: “The Lord our God, the Lord is One” — Deuteronomy 6:4) and strongly rejects any Trinitarian formula.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the “Outline three…” question, give three clearly separate points about the Six Beliefs or Five Roots — do not write one extended explanation of a single belief. Each point should be distinct and identifiable. For the 5-mark “Explain two… with sources” question, the fifth mark depends on naming a specific source: Kitab al-iman 1:4 or Surah 112 are strong anchors for Tawhid and the Six Beliefs. On the 12-mark Discuss question, the most common failure is treating the Sunni–Shi’a comparison as a single brief sentence — both frameworks deserve developed, sourced explanation. SPaG marks are available on selected 12-mark questions: spell Tawhid, Usul ad-Din, Shirk and Adalat correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sunni Muslims hold the Six Beliefs of Islam (Allah, Angels, Books, Prophets, Day of Judgement, Predestination), drawn from Kitab al-iman 1:4; Shi’a Muslims organise belief around the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din (Tawhid, Adl, Nubuwwah, Imamah, Mi’ad).
  • Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is the foundation of all Islamic belief. Surah 112 is the key Qur’anic text; Shirk (associating partners with Allah) is the only unforgivable sin.
  • The key Shi’a differences are: Adl (Divine Justice) replaces al-Qadr as a named Root, and Imamah (divinely appointed leadership) is added; Twelver Shi’a follow twelve Imams while Sevener (Ismaili) Shi’a follow seven.

practice_questions.text: Outline three of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: belief in Allah (Tawhid); belief in angels (Malaikah); belief in the holy books (Kutub); belief in the prophets (Risalah); belief in the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din); belief in predestination (al-Qadr). One mark per discrete belief named — three separate points required.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims believe about the nature of Allah.
practice_questions.model_answer: Muslims believe Allah is omnipotent (all-powerful), merciful (expressed through the names Ar-Rahman and Ar-Rahim) and just. He is both transcendent (beyond and above creation) and immanent (intimately close to believers). He is absolutely one (Tawhid) with no partners or equals. Three clear points earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Sunni and Shi'a core beliefs.
practice_questions.model_answer: First difference: Sunni belief includes al-Qadr (predestination) as the sixth article, while Shi'a Islam replaces this with Adl (Divine Justice) in the Five Roots of Usul ad-Din. Shi'a scholars emphasise Allah's justice to uphold human moral accountability. Second difference: Shi'a Islam includes Imamah (divinely appointed leadership through the Prophet's family) as a Root of Religion, which has no direct equivalent in the Sunni Six Beliefs. This reflects the Shi'a conviction that Ali and his descendants were the rightful leaders after Muhammad. Two developed points, two marks each.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Tawhid is important for Muslims.
In your answer you must refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.model_answer: First reason: Tawhid shapes every aspect of a Muslim's worship and daily life. Because Allah is absolutely one, no prayer, loyalty or devotion may be directed anywhere else. Surah 112 declares 'He is Allah, the One. Allah is Eternal and Absolute' — this verse is recited daily by Muslims as an affirmation of their faith. Second reason: Belief in Tawhid defines what counts as sin. The opposite of Tawhid is Shirk (associating partners with Allah), described in the Qur'an as the only unforgivable sin if not repented of. This conviction shapes Islamic art, architecture and practice. The fifth mark requires the named source — Surah 112 is the expected anchor.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'The Sunni Six Beliefs and the Shi'a Five Roots of Usul ad-Din are more alike than they are different.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support (more alike): Both frameworks share the three central convictions of Tawhid (oneness of Allah), Nubuwwah (prophethood, including Muhammad as the final prophet) and belief in judgement/resurrection. Both ground these convictions in the Qur'an and the Sunnah. The shared emphasis on Tawhid means that in daily worship, prayer and ethical life, Sunni and Shi'a Muslims are largely indistinguishable. A Muslim who accepts the Six Beliefs effectively accepts four of the Five Roots without alteration. Arguments against (more different): The two frameworks diverge on foundational questions. Shi'a Islam replaces al-Qadr with Adl — this is not a minor variation but a theological commitment to Divine Justice that shapes how Shi'a Muslims understand human freedom and moral accountability. Imamah is even more distinctive: it introduces the concept of divinely guided Imams from the Prophet's family (Ahl-ul-Bayt), which has no equivalent in the Sunni six-article framework. For Shi'a Muslims, especially Twelvers, belief in the Hidden Imam and the expectation of his return are central to religious identity in ways the Six Beliefs do not capture. The Sevener/Twelver split further diversifies Shi'a belief. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might note that the two frameworks share more at the level of doctrine about God and revelation than they do at the level of religious authority. Tawhid is identical; what divides the traditions most is Imamah — a belief about who leads the community, not a belief about the nature of God. This suggests the statement is broadly true about God-belief but misleading about the institutional and political dimensions of faith. Mastering (10-12): both sides developed with named sources; weighs perspectives; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides present, one source, conclusion present. Developing (4-6): one side dominant, sources vague. Emerging (1-3): brief, one-sided, no sources.

practice_questions.text: Outline three qualities or characteristics of Allah as described in Islamic teaching.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: omnipotence (Allah is all-powerful); beneficence (Allah is supremely good and generous); mercy (expressed through Ar-Rahman — universal mercy — and Ar-Rahim — particular mercy for believers); transcendence (Allah is beyond and above the physical world); immanence (Allah is intimately close to creation). One mark per clearly distinct quality.

lessons.title: Risalah, Holy Books, Angels and Predestination
lessons.description: Prophets including Adam, Ibrahim and Muhammad; the Qur'an and other holy books; angels Jibril, Izra'il and Mika'il; al-Qadr.
lessons.content_html:
Risalah — Prophethood

Risalah means prophethood. Muslims believe Allah did not leave humanity without guidance — He sent prophets to every nation at different times throughout history. Prophets are human beings chosen by Allah; they are not divine, but they are sinless (ma’sum) in the delivery of their message and are perfectly obedient to God. The Qur’an names 25 prophets, though Muslim tradition holds there were many more. Surah 2:136 instructs believers: “We believe in Allah and what was revealed to us and what was revealed to Ibrahim, Isma’il, Ishaq, Ya’qub, and the Tribes — and what was given to Musa and Isa and all the other prophets from their Lord. We make no distinction between any of them.”

Adam was the first human and the first prophet. Allah created Adam from clay and breathed life into him. In Islam, Adam’s sin in the Garden is not inherited by humanity — he repented, was forgiven, and every person is born in a state of fitrah (natural purity). There is no doctrine of original sin in Islam.

Ibrahim (Abraham) is known as Khalilullah — the Friend of Allah. He demonstrated perfect submission by being willing to sacrifice his son when commanded by Allah, who intervened and provided a ram instead. Most Muslim scholars identify the son as Isma’il, though the Qur’an does not name him in this narrative. Ibrahim also rebuilt the Ka’aba in Makkah with Isma’il, establishing the site of annual pilgrimage.

Musa (Moses) received the Tawrat (Torah) and led the Israelites from Egypt. Dawud (David) received the Zabur (Psalms). Isa (Jesus) received the Injil (Gospel) and is regarded in Islam as one of the greatest prophets — born of the virgin Maryam through divine intervention, the Messiah, who performed miracles by Allah’s permission.

Muhammad (born c.570 CE, died 632 CE) is the final prophet — the Seal of the Prophets (Khatam an-Nabiyyin). No prophet will follow him. He received the Qur’an through the angel Jibril over approximately 23 years, beginning in 610 CE. The Hijra (migration from Makkah to Madinah) in 622 CE marks the start of the Islamic calendar.

Key Fact

Surah 2:136 is the Edexcel-named anchor for Risalah. It establishes that Muslims believe in all prophets without distinction — this is what sets Islamic prophethood apart from the idea that only one tradition’s prophets matter. Surah 16:35–36 reinforces this, stating Allah sent a messenger to every nation commanding worship of Him alone.

Kutub — The Holy Books

Kutub means the holy books or scriptures. Muslims believe Allah revealed guidance to humanity through a series of scriptures. Surah 5:43–48 describes how each community received its own scripture and should live by it: “We revealed the Torah, containing guidance and light… We sent Isa, son of Maryam, in their footsteps… and gave him the Injil.” The passage goes on to say the Qur’an was sent to confirm and safeguard what came before.

Tawrat (Torah) — revealed to Musa (Moses). Muslims believe the original Tawrat was the word of Allah, but that it has been altered over time by human hands.

Zabur (Psalms) — revealed to Dawud (David). Again, Muslims hold the original to have been divine but believe the present form is not perfectly preserved.

Injil (Gospel) — revealed to Isa (Jesus). Muslims believe Isa received a pure revelation from Allah, distinct from the four Gospels in the New Testament, which are regarded as human accounts rather than the original divine text.

Qur’an — revealed to Muhammad through the angel Jibril over 23 years. Muslims believe the Qur’an is the final, complete and perfectly preserved word of Allah. Unlike previous scriptures, it has not been changed. Sahifah (scrolls) were also revealed to Ibrahim and Adam but are not preserved as independent texts today.

Malaikah — Angels

Malaikah (angels) are an article of faith in both Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Muslims believe angels were created from divine light, have no free will, do not eat or sleep, and obey Allah perfectly. They are neither male nor female. Believing in the angels is the second of the Six Beliefs of Sunni Islam.

Jibril (Gabriel) is the most important angel in Islamic teaching. He delivered the Qur’anic revelation to Muhammad and brought divine messages to earlier prophets including Ibrahim and Isa. He is known as the “trustworthy spirit” in the Qur’an.

Izra’il is the angel of death. Surah 32:11 refers to him: “The Angel of Death, who has been given charge of you, will take your souls.” Muslims believe Izra’il takes the soul from the body at the appointed moment of death — a moment pre-determined only by Allah.

Mika’il (Michael) is associated with mercy, rain, provisions and natural sustenance. He is responsible for the weather and natural phenomena that sustain life on earth.

Two further angels, Munkar and Nakir, are believed to question the deceased in the grave about their faith. Israfil is the angel who will blow the trumpet on the Day of Judgement.

Key Fact

Surah 32:11 is the Edexcel-named anchor for belief in the angel Izra’il (the Angel of Death): “The Angel of Death, who has been given charge of you, will take your souls.” This verse connects Malaikah (angels) to Akhirah (the afterlife) — the angel’s role at death is the first step in the journey to judgement.

Al-Qadr — Predestination

Al-Qadr is the sixth article of Sunni faith. It means predestination — the belief that Allah has complete knowledge of past, present and future, and that everything that happens is within His will. A hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 states that an angel records four things about a person before birth: their provision, their lifespan, their deeds, and whether they will be fortunate or unfortunate. This is written on the “Preserved Tablet” (Lawh al-Mahfuz).

A common misconception is that al-Qadr means humans are puppets with no real choices. Most Sunni Muslims hold that Allah’s foreknowledge is absolute — He knows what every person will do before they do it — but that His knowing does not cause the action. Humans genuinely choose; they simply cannot surprise God. This is how human accountability on the Day of Judgement is preserved.

Shi’a Islam approaches this differently. Rather than naming al-Qadr as a Root of Religion, Shi’a theology names Adl (Divine Justice) — emphasising that because Allah is perfectly just, He would not hold humans accountable for actions they were forced to perform. This framing places the accent on human freedom and divine justice rather than on divine decree.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 5-mark “Explain two… including a source of wisdom” question on Risalah, the expected source is Surah 2:136 (belief in all prophets without distinction) or Surah 5:43–48 (on the revealed books). For questions on angels, cite Surah 32:11 to anchor the role of Izra’il. For al-Qadr, Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 is the named hadith anchor. On the 12-mark Discuss, a common failure is writing only about one prophet or one holy book — the spec expects you to show knowledge of the system of prophethood as a whole. The 5-mark source-of-wisdom mark depends on naming the reference: a vague mention of “the Qur’an” without a surah does not earn that fifth mark. SPaG marks reward correct spelling of Risalah, Malaikah, al-Qadr and Kutub.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Risalah (prophethood) holds that Allah sent messengers to every nation; key prophets include Adam, Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, Isa and Muhammad. Surah 2:136 states that Muslims believe in all prophets equally. Muhammad, born c.570 CE, is the final Seal of the Prophets.
  • The holy books (Kutub) include the Tawrat, Zabur, Injil and Sahifah — all believed to be divine in origin but not perfectly preserved. The Qur’an is the final, complete and perfectly preserved revelation, confirmed by Surah 5:43–48.
  • The three named angels are Jibril (revelation), Izra’il (death — Surah 32:11) and Mika’il (mercy/sustenance). Al-Qadr (predestination) is the sixth Sunni belief; Sahih al-Bukhari 78:685 records that four things about each person are recorded before birth. Shi’a Islam replaces al-Qadr with Adl (Divine Justice).

One mark per named prophet with one identifying detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims believe about the holy books (Kutub).
practice_questions.model_answer: Muslims believe Allah revealed scriptures to different prophets at different times, including the Tawrat to Musa, the Zabur to Dawud and the Injil to Isa. These earlier books are believed to have been altered over time. The Qur'an, revealed to Muhammad, is the final, complete and perfectly preserved word of Allah. Three clear descriptive points earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why belief in prophethood (Risalah) is important for Muslims.
practice_questions.model_answer: First reason: Risalah shows that Allah cares for humanity and has never left people without guidance. By sending prophets to every nation, Allah ensured that all people had access to truth. This reassures Muslims that divine guidance is both universal and merciful. Second reason: Muhammad as the final prophet means that the Qur'an is the complete and unchangeable word of Allah. Nothing further needs to be added. This gives Muslims confidence that their scripture is authentic and authoritative for all time. Two developed explanations, two marks each.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two ways in which angels are important in Islamic belief.
In your answer you must refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.model_answer: First way: Angels connect Allah's will to the physical world. Jibril delivered the Qur'anic revelation directly to the Prophet Muhammad, making the angel essential to how Islam's holy scripture came to exist. Without Jibril, there would be no Qur'an in its present form. Second way: Angels are involved in the transition from this life to the next. Surah 32:11 states: 'The Angel of Death, who has been given charge of you, will take your souls' — this is Izra'il, whose role confirms that death is in Allah's hands, not a random event. This connects belief in angels to belief in the afterlife (Akhirah). The fifth mark requires the named source — Surah 32:11 is the expected anchor.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'The Qur'an is more important to Muslims than any other source of authority.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support: The Qur'an is the direct, final and perfectly preserved word of Allah, revealed to Muhammad through Jibril. Surah 5:43-48 describes it as the guardian and confirmation of all earlier scriptures. Unlike the Tawrat, Zabur and Injil, the Qur'an has not been altered by human hands — Muslims believe it remains exactly as revealed. It is recited in prayer five times daily, memorised by millions, and governs Islamic law (Shari'ah). No other source can claim the same direct divine authority. Arguments against: The Sunnah (the Prophet's example, recorded in the Hadith collections including Sahih al-Bukhari) is considered essential for interpreting the Qur'an. Without the Hadith, many Qur'anic commands would be impossible to apply in practice — for example, the Qur'an instructs Muslims to pray but does not specify the exact movements; those come from the Sunnah. For Shi'a Muslims, the authority of the Imam also carries significant weight in interpreting revelation. The Qur'an itself states that Muhammad was sent to explain its teachings to humanity (Surah 16:44), suggesting the Sunnah is integral rather than secondary. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might note that the Qur'an is the highest source in theory — its status as the uncreated word of Allah is undisputed — but in practice Muslims cannot fully live by the Qur'an without the Sunnah as an interpretive guide. The two together form the primary sources of Islamic authority. Mastering (10-12): both sides developed with named Qur'anic anchors; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides present; one source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant; vague sources. Emerging (1-3): brief and one-sided.

lessons.title: Akhirah: Life After Death and the Day of Judgement
lessons.description: Muslim teaching on judgment, paradise and hell, and how belief in the afterlife shapes Muslim life.
lessons.content_html:
Akhirah — Belief in Life After Death

Akhirah means “the hereafter” or life after death. It is one of the core beliefs in both Sunni and Shi’a Islam. Muslims believe that this earthly life is temporary — a test and a preparation. The real, eternal life begins after death. Everything a person does in this life will be examined on the Day of Judgement (Yawm al-Din).

Surah 17:49–72 addresses the question of resurrection directly. The passage confronts the sceptical claim that decayed bones could not be revived, and asserts that Allah, who created humanity the first time, is entirely capable of creating again. The surah describes the journey of the soul after death, from initial disbelief through to the scales of judgement, the record of deeds and the dividing of humanity into those destined for Jannah and those for Jahannam.

Key Fact

Akhirah is a likely anchor for 12-mark Discuss questions that ask you to compare Islamic and another tradition’s views of the afterlife. Surah 17:49–72 is the named Qur’anic anchor for Muslim teaching on resurrection and judgement.

Death and the Barzakh

After death, Muslims believe the soul enters Barzakh (the barrier or intermediate state). In Barzakh, the soul waits until the Day of Judgement. During this time, two angels — Munkar and Nakir — are believed to question the deceased about their faith. The righteous experience a peaceful Barzakh; those who have done wrong may experience suffering.

The Day of Judgement

On the Day of Judgement, the angel Israfil will blow a trumpet, all of creation will be destroyed and then all people will be resurrected. Every person will stand before Allah and give an account of their life. Islamic teaching describes several features of this judgement:

  • Each person’s deeds are recorded by the angels Kiraman Katibin (“noble scribes”) throughout their life.
  • The Mizan (scales) will weigh every person’s good and bad deeds.
  • Each person will receive a record of their deeds — in their right hand (those destined for paradise) or behind their back or in their left hand (those destined for hell).
  • The Sirat (the bridge over hell) must be crossed. The righteous cross it easily; the wicked fall into Jahannam.

Jannah — Paradise

Jannah is the Islamic concept of paradise — a place of eternal peace, beauty and fulfilment. The Qur’an describes Jannah in vivid terms: cool shade, flowing rivers, rich provision, companionship and, most importantly, the direct experience of Allah’s presence (the Beatific Vision-equivalent in Islamic theology, called ru’yat Allah). Entry to Jannah is by Allah’s mercy, not by human deeds alone — deeds are the indicator of faith, but the final decision belongs to Allah.

Jahannam — Hell

Jahannam is the Islamic concept of hell. It is described in the Qur’an as a place of fire and suffering. Muslim scholars differ on whether Jahannam is eternal for all its inhabitants. Sunni mainstream views hold that non-believers remain in hell permanently, while some Muslims who have sinned but still held faith may be punished for a time before ultimately entering Jannah by Allah’s mercy. Jahannam is not described as a place of torture for its own sake — it is described as the natural consequence of a life lived in rejection of Allah.

Belief in Akhirah motivates Muslims to act ethically in the knowledge that everything they do is being recorded. It gives purpose to suffering: if life is a test, hardship has meaning. It provides comfort in the face of death and injustice — even if wrongs are not righted in this life, they will be addressed by Allah on the Day of Judgement. It also encourages generosity and justice, since how a person treats others will be weighed on the Mizan.

Examiners may ask you to compare Islamic and another tradition’s afterlife beliefs in a 12-mark Discuss question.

  • Islam: physical resurrection on the Day of Judgement; deeds weighed on the Mizan; Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell) as eternal destinations. Entry to Jannah is by Allah’s mercy. No concept of reincarnation.
  • Catholic Christianity: resurrection of the body at the Last Judgement; Purgatory as an intermediate state of purification for the faithful; Heaven, Purgatory and Hell as possible destinations. The Catechism of the Catholic Church (CCC 1030–1032) describes Purgatory. Islam has no equivalent to Purgatory, though the concept of Barzakh shares some structural similarity as an intermediate state.
  • Hinduism/Buddhism (for contrast): reincarnation (samsara) and the eventual release from the cycle (moksha/nirvana). Islam and Christianity both reject reincarnation.
lessons.exam_tip_html: This spec point is starred (1.8*), which means it is a likely source of 12-mark Discuss questions requiring comparison with another tradition. When writing a Discuss answer on Akhirah, develop the Islamic view fully first with Surah 17:49–72 as your named anchor, then compare with Christian or another tradition’s afterlife teaching with equal depth — examiners consistently note that the “other side” is underdeveloped. The 5-mark source-of-wisdom mark: “a verse of the Qur’an” does not earn it; you need Surah 17 or a specific reference. SPaG marks: spell Akhirah, Jannah, Jahannam and Barzakh correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Akhirah (the afterlife) is a core Islamic belief: death is followed by Barzakh (the intermediate state), then resurrection, the Day of Judgement, and either Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell). Surah 17:49–72 is the named Qur’anic anchor for this teaching.
  • On the Day of Judgement, all deeds are weighed on the Mizan (scales); each person receives a record of their deeds. Entry to Jannah is ultimately by Allah’s mercy; Jahannam is the consequence of rejecting faith.
  • Belief in Akhirah shapes Muslim ethics, motivating good deeds and providing comfort in suffering. This is a starred spec point (1.8*) — compare Islamic afterlife belief with another tradition for the 12-mark Discuss question.

This provides a constant incentive to act honestly, generously and justly, even when no human observer is present. Second way: Belief in Akhirah provides comfort in suffering. If this life is a test and injustice will be addressed by Allah's final judgement, then suffering in this world has meaning and wrongs will ultimately be righted. practice_questions.model_answer: First belief: Jannah is a place of eternal peace and fulfilment, described in the Qur'an as a garden with flowing rivers, abundant provision and companionship. Surah 17:49-72 addresses the resurrection that precedes entry into Jannah, stating that Allah who created humanity the first time is capable of creating again. Second belief: Entry into Jannah is ultimately by Allah's mercy, not by human deeds alone. A person's deeds are an indicator of faith, but the final decision belongs to Allah. This underlines Islamic teaching that humans are utterly dependent on divine mercy, not entitled to paradise by their own achievements. The fifth mark requires Surah 17 as the named anchor.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'Belief in life after death is the most important belief in Islam.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support: Akhirah gives meaning to every aspect of Muslim life. If there is no judgement, there is no ultimate basis for ethics — why act justly if injustice goes unpunished? The Qur'an repeatedly connects moral commands to the reality of the Day of Judgement, suggesting that the afterlife is the engine of Islamic ethics. Surah 17:49-72 asserts that resurrection is as certain as the first act of creation. For millions of Muslims, the awareness of being watched and recorded gives daily life its moral seriousness. Arguments against: Tawhid — the absolute oneness of Allah — is arguably more foundational. Before any question of afterlife arises, a Muslim must believe that there is one God who created, sustains and judges. Without Tawhid, there is no framework within which Akhirah makes sense. Moreover, the Five Pillars (the practical obligations of Islam) are not primarily about preparing for death — they are about continuous submission to Allah in this life: through Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (daily prayer), Zakah (charity), Sawm (fasting) and Hajj (pilgrimage). Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that Tawhid is logically prior to Akhirah — without belief in one just God, the concept of a Day of Judgement has no force. But in terms of day-to-day impact on Muslim behaviour, belief in Akhirah is exceptionally powerful. The statement is defensible but not the only tenable position. Mastering (10-12): both sides with Qur'anic anchors; explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant; vague. Emerging (1-3): brief and one-sided.

lessons.title: The Five Pillars and Ten Obligatory Acts
lessons.description: Shahadah, Salah, Sawm, Zakah and Hajj; the Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi'a Islam; Khums.
lessons.content_html:
The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam

Islam is built on five core practices known as the Five Pillars. These are not optional extras — they are fard (compulsory) for every adult Muslim of sound mind. Together they shape a Muslim’s daily life, social relationships and relationship with Allah. The Prophet Muhammad described Islam as being “built upon five things” (Hadith, Sahih al-Bukhari). Surah 3:17–21 praises those who are patient, truthful, devout, and charitable — qualities embodied by the Five Pillars.

Key Fact

The Five Pillars: Shahadah (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakah (2.5% of savings given to those in need), Sawm (fasting during Ramadan), Hajj (pilgrimage to Makkah at least once). This is the foundational framework of Sunni practice.

Shahadah — Declaration of Faith

The Shahadah is the declaration: “There is no God but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah.” It is the most fundamental act of Islamic faith. Reciting it sincerely and with understanding is the act that makes a person Muslim. It is whispered in a newborn’s ear, said at regular intervals in prayer and at the hour of death. Surah 3:17–21 describes those who consistently bear witness (“shahada”) to Allah’s oneness as among the most praiseworthy of believers.

Salah — Prayer

Salah is compulsory prayer five times a day: Fajr (before sunrise), Zuhr (after midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (after sunset) and Isha (night). Before praying, Muslims perform wudu (ritual washing). On Fridays, Sunni Muslim men are expected to pray Jummah (the Friday congregational prayer) at the mosque. Surah 29:45 states: “Recite what has been revealed to you of the Scripture; keep up the prayer — prayer restrains outrageous and unacceptable behaviour.” Surah 15:98–99 connects glorification of Allah in prayer with certainty of faith. Shi’a Muslims perform the same five prayers but may combine them into three prayer times during the day.

Sawm — Fasting

Sawm involves complete fasting during the holy month of Ramadan. Muslims abstain from all food, drink, smoking and sexual relations from dawn to sunset. Surah 2:183–185 commands: “You who believe, fasting is prescribed for you, as it was prescribed for those before you, so that you may be mindful of God.” Within Ramadan, the Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power) commemorates the first revelation of the Qur’an to Muhammad and is described in the Qur’an as better than a thousand months of worship. Those who cannot fast (due to illness, pregnancy or travel) may break their fast and compensate later. Ramadan ends with the festival of Id-ul-Fitr.

Zakah — Almsgiving

Zakah means “purification” or “growth.” It requires every Muslim whose savings exceed the nisab (minimum threshold) to give 2.5% of their annual savings to those in need. Surah 9:58–60 specifies eight categories of those entitled to receive Zakah, including the poor, the indebted and travellers in need. Zakah purifies the giver’s remaining wealth from greed, supports the poor and reduces inequality within the ummah (global Muslim community).

Hajj — Pilgrimage

Hajj takes place in the twelfth month of the Islamic calendar and must be performed at least once in a lifetime by every Muslim who is physically and financially able. Surah 2:124–130 describes Ibrahim and Isma’il building the Ka’aba and establishing the rites of pilgrimage. Surah 22:25–30 describes the sacred sites and the command to proclaim Hajj to all people. Hajj rites include walking around the Ka’aba seven times (tawaf), walking between the hills of Safa and Marwa, standing on the plain of Arafat (wuquf), and symbolically stoning the devil. Hajj creates a profound sense of equality and unity — all pilgrims wear identical white garments (ihram), erasing distinctions of wealth and rank.

  • Islam: Salah is compulsory five times daily; all pray in Arabic using set movements; facing Makkah (qibla); preceded by wudu. Jummah (Friday prayer) is a communal obligation for men.
  • Catholic Christianity: The Mass is the central act of worship — the Eucharist (the source and summit of Catholic life, Lumen Gentium 7). Catholics attend Sunday Mass as an obligation. Prayer takes many forms: formal (the Divine Office) and informal. No single fixed time structure equivalent to the five daily prayers.
  • General Christianity: Worship varies widely — liturgical (set structure, e.g. Anglican) and non-liturgical (free-form, e.g. Baptist). Prayer is encouraged but not prescribed at fixed times in the way Islamic Salah is.

The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam

Shi’a Muslims have their own framework of obligatory acts. While the Five Pillars are broadly shared, Shi’a Islam lists Ten Obligatory Acts (Furu ad-Din — branches of religion). These include Salah, Sawm, Zakah and Hajj (shared with Sunni Islam), but add several distinctively Shi’a duties: Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad (striving in the way of Allah), Amr-bil-Maroof (commanding what is right), and Nahy-anil-Munkar (forbidding what is wrong). Khums is particularly significant: Surah 8:41 specifies that a fifth of certain gains should be set aside “for Allah and the Messenger,” which Shi’a Muslims understand as a continuing obligation paid to the Imam’s representatives (the religious scholars).

Key Fact

Khums (20% of surplus income) is a Shi’a-specific obligation distinct from Sunni Zakah (2.5% of savings above nisab). Khums is paid to the Imam’s representatives (religious scholars) for religious and charitable purposes. Both Zakah and Khums serve to reduce inequality within the ummah, but they operate on different rates and through different channels.

The Five Pillars are the universal Sunni framework of practice. The Ten Obligatory Acts of Shi’a Islam (Wajibat) include the Five Pillars (Salah, Sawm, Zakah, Hajj, and Shahadah through Walayah) plus additional obligations: Khums (20% levy), Jihad, commanding good, forbidding evil, and love/disavowal (Tawallah and Tabarra). Some scholars count the Ten differently, but Khums is the most distinctive Shi’a addition to this framework. The underlying logic is the same: both Sunni and Shi’a Muslims structure their lives around prescribed acts of worship that express submission to Allah.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For 5-mark “Explain two… with sources” questions on Islamic practice, use these named anchors: Salah — Surah 29:45 or Surah 15:98–99; Sawm — Surah 2:183–185; Zakah — Surah 9:58–60; Hajj — Surah 2:124–130 or Surah 22:25–30. For the 12-mark Discuss on worship (2.3*), develop both Islamic and another tradition’s practice with equal depth — the Sunni–Shi’a difference on Salah (three times vs five) and on obligatory acts (Five Pillars vs Ten Obligatory Acts including Khums) is a rich source of developed contrast. The most common failure is a Discuss answer that treats “another point of view” as a single brief sentence. SPaG: spell Shahadah, Zakah, Ramadan and Khums correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Five Pillars of Sunni Islam are Shahadah, Salah, Zakah (2.5% of savings), Sawm (fasting in Ramadan, commanded in Surah 2:183–185) and Hajj to Makkah (anchored in Surah 2:124–130 and Surah 22:25–30).
  • Shi’a Islam has Ten Obligatory Acts (Furu ad-Din), adding Khums (20% of surplus income), Jihad, and duties to command good and forbid evil — making Khums a key Sunni–Shi’a difference in practice.
  • Salah (2.3*) is a starred spec point: Sunni Muslims pray five times daily; Shi’a may combine into three times. Hajj creates equality through ihram. The Friday congregational prayer (Jummah) is obligatory for adult Sunni Muslim men.

One mark per clearly distinct pillar with its English meaning.

practice_questions.text: Describe the significance of Hajj for Muslims.
practice_questions.model_answer: Hajj is the fifth pillar of Islam and compulsory at least once for Muslims who are able. It takes place in Makkah, the holiest city in Islam. Pilgrims wear identical white garments (ihram), symbolising equality before Allah. Hajj commemorates the actions of Ibrahim and Isma'il. It unites Muslims globally and spiritually renews the individual. Three descriptive points earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two differences between Sunni and Shi'a obligations in Islamic practice.
practice_questions.model_answer: First difference: Sunni Islam has the Five Pillars; Shi'a Islam has Ten Obligatory Acts (Furu ad-Din). The Shi'a framework adds Khums (a 20% tax on surplus income), Jihad as an obligation, and duties to command good and forbid wrong. This reflects Shi'a theology's emphasis on active social justice and the role of the Imam's representatives. Second difference: The Zakah rate differs. Sunni Zakah is 2.5% of savings above the nisab. Shi'a Khums is 20% of surplus income, paid to religious scholars acting as representatives of the Imam. This difference in rate and recipient reflects the distinct Shi'a belief in Imamah and the ongoing role of religious leadership. Two developed points, two marks each.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why Salah is important for Muslims.
In your answer you must refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.model_answer: First reason: Salah structures a Muslim's day around remembrance of Allah. By praying five times daily, a Muslim is reminded of Allah's presence throughout every activity. Surah 29:45 states: 'Keep up the prayer — prayer restrains outrageous and unacceptable behaviour.' This shows that Salah is not merely ritual — it actively shapes moral conduct. Second reason: Salah unites the global ummah. Whether praying in London, Jakarta or Cairo, all Muslims face the qibla (Makkah), pray in Arabic and follow the same movements. This creates a profound sense of shared identity. The fifth mark requires Surah 29:45 as the named anchor.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'The Five Pillars are all equally important for Muslims.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support: Each pillar addresses a different but essential dimension of Muslim faith and practice. Shahadah establishes identity; Salah maintains daily contact with God; Zakah expresses social responsibility; Sawm builds spiritual discipline; Hajj connects the believer to Islamic origins and the global ummah. Neglecting any one weakens the others — as the Hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari suggests, Islam is built on all five. Together they form an integrated structure, not a hierarchy. Arguments against: The Shahadah is often described as the most fundamental, since it is the act of becoming Muslim and is embedded within every other pillar. Without affirming the oneness of Allah and the prophethood of Muhammad, the other four pillars are meaningless. Some scholars prioritise Salah as the pillar that is most regularly practised and that most consistently shapes Muslim identity. Hajj is the only pillar many Muslims never perform (due to financial or health constraints), and exemptions exist for Sawm — suggesting these are contextually flexible in ways Salah and Zakah are not. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that the Shahadah is logically primary (it defines what it means to be Muslim) but that in terms of daily impact, Salah is the most shaping practice. The pillars are interdependent rather than strictly equal in weight — their importance varies by context and by individual circumstance. Mastering (10-12): both sides with named sources (Sahih al-Bukhari, Surah references); weighing explicit; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; one source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant. Emerging (1-3): brief and one-sided.

lessons.title: Jihad and Islamic Festivals
lessons.description: Lesser and greater Jihad; Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, Id-ul-Ghadeer and Ashura.
lessons.content_html:
Jihad — Striving in the Way of Allah

The word jihad means “struggle” or “striving.” It does not mean “holy war” — that is a common mistranslation. Every Muslim is engaged in jihad whenever they strive to be a better person, resist temptation, act justly or work for a fairer society. Islam recognises two forms of jihad: greater jihad (al-jihad al-akbar) and lesser jihad (al-jihad al-asghar).

Key Fact

Greater jihad is the struggle against nafs (the lower self) — the daily effort to be honest, compassionate, self-disciplined and obedient to Allah. Classical scholars held that this inward struggle is the most difficult and most continuous form of jihad. Lesser jihad refers to defensive struggle to protect the Muslim community under conditions tightly constrained by Islamic jurisprudence.

Greater Jihad — The Inner Struggle

Greater jihad involves resisting the temptation to lie, be selfish, be unjust or neglect religious duties. It includes studying Islam, raising a family according to Islamic values, working honestly, caring for parents and being a good neighbour. Every act of worship — Salah, Sawm, Zakah — is itself a form of greater jihad, since each requires the believer to overcome laziness, selfishness or distraction to submit to Allah. Greater jihad is lifelong; it ends only at death.

Lesser Jihad — Conditions and Constraints

Lesser jihad refers to the use of force to defend the Muslim community, resist oppression or uphold justice. It is not a licence for aggression. Surah 2:190–194 sets clear conditions: “Fight in the way of Allah those who fight you but do not transgress, for Allah does not love transgressors.” The passage prohibits fighting those who do not fight, prohibits attacking during sacred months and commands that fighting must stop when the enemy ceases hostilities. Surah 22:39 permits Muslims who have been wronged to fight in self-defence: “Permission to fight is given to those who have been attacked.”

Classical Islamic jurisprudence lists conditions that must be met before lesser jihad is permissible:

  • There must be a legitimate cause — typically self-defence or the defence of those being oppressed.
  • All peaceful alternatives must have been exhausted first.
  • It must be declared by a legitimate authority (not by individuals acting alone).
  • Non-combatants — women, children, the elderly, clergy and those not fighting — must be protected. Destruction of crops and buildings is prohibited.
  • It must cease when the enemy stops fighting or offers peace (Surah 2:192–193).

These conditions mean that lesser jihad is constrained in classical Islamic teaching far more than media portrayals often suggest. Extremist interpretations that remove these conditions are rejected by mainstream Islamic scholars.

Reducing jihad to “holy war” misrepresents Islamic teaching in two ways. First, it ignores greater jihad, which classical scholars considered the more important form. Second, it strips lesser jihad of its strict conditions — making it sound like permission for unlimited violence, which the Qur’an explicitly prohibits. Surah 2:190 states: “do not transgress, for Allah does not love transgressors.” Exam answers that describe jihad only as “holy war” will score poorly; both forms must be covered.

Islamic Festivals

Islamic festivals unite the global ummah in shared acts of worship, remembrance and celebration. Four key festivals feature in the specification: Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Fitr, Id-ul-Ghadeer (Shi’a) and Ashura.

Id-ul-Adha — Festival of Sacrifice

Id-ul-Adha (the Festival of Sacrifice) is one of the two major Islamic festivals. It commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son at Allah’s command. Surah 37:77–111 recounts the story: Ibrahim was commanded in a dream to sacrifice his son; he informed his son, who submitted willingly. As Ibrahim prepared to act, Allah intervened and provided a ram as a substitute, rewarding Ibrahim’s faith with the announcement that he had fulfilled the vision. Most Muslim scholars identify the son as Isma’il, though the Qur’an does not name him in this passage — the identification is traditional, not explicitly stated. Id-ul-Adha takes place during the Hajj period and involves the sacrifice of an animal (qurbani), with meat shared among family, friends and the poor.

Id-ul-Fitr — Festival Marking the End of Ramadan

Id-ul-Fitr celebrates the successful completion of the month-long Ramadan fast. It begins with a communal prayer and sermon at the mosque. Muslims give Zakat al-Fitr (a special obligatory charity at Ramadan’s end) so that everyone in the community can celebrate. The festival continues with visiting family, feasting, wearing new or clean clothes, and giving gifts to children. Id-ul-Fitr is a celebration of gratitude to Allah for the strength to complete Sawm and a joyful acknowledgement of the community that fasted together.

Id-ul-Ghadeer — A Shi’a Festival

Id-ul-Ghadeer is one of the most important Shi’a festivals. It commemorates the event at Ghadir Khumm (on the return from the Prophet’s final Hajj in 632 CE) when, according to Shi’a belief, the Prophet Muhammad announced that Ali ibn Abi Talib was to be his rightful successor. Shi’a Muslims understand Surah 5:3 — “Today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My blessing upon you” — as referring to this proclamation at Ghadir. Sunni Muslims interpret this verse differently, associating it with the completion of the Hajj rather than a specific designation of Ali. Id-ul-Ghadeer is therefore a specifically Shi’a festival with profound significance for the doctrine of Imamah.

Ashura — A Day of Contrasting Significance

Ashura falls on the tenth day of Muharram (the first month of the Islamic calendar) and holds very different significance for Sunni and Shi’a Muslims.

Sunni Ashura: For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is primarily a day of voluntary fasting. A hadith recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari reports that when the Prophet arrived in Madinah and observed the Jewish community fasting, he was told it was the day Moses was saved from Pharaoh. The Prophet reportedly said he had a stronger connection to Moses and encouraged fasting on this day. It is an act of gratitude rather than mourning.

Shi’a Ashura: For Shi’a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year — a day of mourning and lamentation for the martyrdom of Imam Husayn (the grandson of the Prophet Muhammad and the third Shi’a Imam) at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Husayn and his small band were killed by the forces of Caliph Yazid after refusing to pledge allegiance to what Shi’a Muslims regard as an unjust ruler. Ashura is marked with processions, passionate re-enactments (ta’ziyeh), lamentations and the retelling of Husayn’s sacrifice. The tragedy of Karbala is central to Shi’a religious identity and theology.

Key Fact

Islamic festivals in this spec: Id-ul-Fitr (end of Ramadan — Sunni and Shi’a), Id-ul-Adha (feast of sacrifice, Ibrahim — Sunni and Shi’a), Ashura (Husayn’s martyrdom at Karbala — primarily Shi’a), Id-ul-Ghadeer (Muhammad’s designation of Ali — Shi’a). Surah 37:77–111 is the Qur’anic account of Ibrahim’s sacrifice that Id-ul-Adha commemorates.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The jihad topic is flagged as the highest-risk misconception in the teaching brief. If asked to “outline three aspects of jihad,” you must cover: (1) the meaning of the word (“striving”), (2) greater jihad (inner struggle against nafs), (3) lesser jihad (outward, defensive, under strict conditions). Do not reduce it to “holy war.” For 5-mark “Explain two with sources,” use Surah 2:190–194 for lesser jihad and Surah 22:39 for the permission to defend. For Id-ul-Ghadeer, Surah 5:3 is the Edexcel anchor. For Ashura, name both Sunni (voluntary fast — Sahih al-Bukhari) and Shi’a (Karbala martyrdom) interpretations — examiners expect both. SPaG: spell Jihad, Id-ul-Adha, Id-ul-Ghadeer and Ashura correctly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Jihad means striving: greater jihad (inner spiritual struggle against the lower self) is the continuous, primary form; lesser jihad (outward defence) is constrained by strict conditions including Surah 2:190–194 (no transgression) and Surah 22:39 (only those attacked may fight). Reducing jihad to “holy war” is a misconception.
  • Id-ul-Adha commemorates Ibrahim’s willingness to sacrifice his son (Surah 37:77–111); Id-ul-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan. Both are shared Sunni–Shi’a festivals.
  • Id-ul-Ghadeer (Shi’a) commemorates Muhammad’s announcement of Ali as successor at Ghadir Khumm — anchored in Surah 5:3. Ashura has contrasting Sunni (fasting/gratitude) and Shi’a (mourning for Imam Husayn at Karbala) meanings.

practice_questions.model_answer: First difference: For Sunni Muslims, Ashura is primarily a day of voluntary fasting. A hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari records that the Prophet observed the fast and encouraged it as a day of gratitude commemorating Moses being saved from Pharaoh. It is an optional act of devotion with no element of mourning. Second difference: For Shi'a Muslims, Ashura is the most solemn day of the year — a day of mourning and lamentation for the martyrdom of Imam Husayn, the Prophet's grandson, at the Battle of Karbala in 680 CE. Shi'a Muslims hold processions, re-enactments and lamentations. This reflects the Shi'a theological significance of Husayn's sacrifice as a defining moment in their religious identity. Two developed points, two marks each.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why greater jihad is considered important in Islam.
In your answer you must refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.model_answer: First reason: Greater jihad is central to personal spiritual development. Every act of worship — prayer, fasting, charity — requires overcoming the lower self (nafs). Without this inner struggle, outward religious practice can become hollow habit. The Qur'an commands believers to strive for God: Surah 22:39 describes the striving of those who have been wronged, but the broader context of the surah is that striving for God encompasses all dimensions of life. Second reason: Greater jihad is the most continuous form of jihad, lasting from birth to death. It cannot be completed and set aside. This makes it, in classical Islamic scholarship, the greater of the two forms. The named source — Surah 2:190-194 constrains lesser jihad with conditions, implying that the unconditioned inner struggle is the more fundamental obligation. The fifth mark requires a named surah reference.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'The true meaning of jihad has been misunderstood by most people.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support: The word jihad in Arabic simply means 'striving' and covers all effort made in the way of Allah — including prayer, charity, care for family and personal self-improvement. Greater jihad (the inner struggle against nafs) is considered by classical scholars to be the more important form. Surah 2:190-194 places strict conditions on lesser jihad, making it a constrained, last-resort defence — not an open call to violence. Media and political discourse has reduced a rich theological concept to a single-dimensional caricature of violence. Many Muslims — scholars and practitioners alike — argue that this misrepresentation harms both the religion and wider social understanding. Arguments against: While the inner-struggle interpretation is important, it would also be wrong to suggest that lesser jihad (outward struggle) is not a genuine part of Islamic teaching. The Qur'an does address defensive warfare directly in Surah 2:190-194 and Surah 22:39. Some Islamic scholars throughout history have emphasised outward jihad in specific historical and political contexts. The statement risks overcorrecting — portraying jihad as purely spiritual and ignoring its legitimate outward dimensions. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might argue that most people have misunderstood jihad by reducing it exclusively to violence, since this ignores the greater jihad and the strict conditions on lesser jihad. However, the statement is slightly too absolute — jihad does include an outward dimension that is genuinely part of Islamic teaching, not an invention of misreaders. The fullest understanding acknowledges both dimensions in their proper relationship. Mastering (10-12): both sides developed with Qur'anic anchors (Surah 2:190-194, Surah 22:39); explicit weighing; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; one source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant. Emerging (1-3): brief.

lessons.title: Sources of Authority and Muslim Identity
lessons.description: The Qur'an, the Prophet Muhammad, Hadith, Shari'ah Law and Sufism; mosque architecture, calligraphy, Muslim identity and charity.
lessons.content_html:
Section 3: Sources of Wisdom and Authority

This lesson covers two major areas: the sources of wisdom and authority that Muslims turn to for guidance, and the forms of expression and ways of life that shape Muslim identity.

The Qur’an as a Source of Authority

The Qur’an is the primary source of authority in Islam. Muslims believe it is the direct, unchanged word of Allah. Surah 53:4–18 is a key Qur’anic verse confirming the Qur’an’s authority: it describes the divine origin of the revelation (“It is nothing less than a revelation that is sent to him”) and the vision of the Prophet during which the revelation was transmitted. The Qur’an is used in daily life: in Salah (prayer recitation is in Arabic), in the home (reading for guidance and blessing), in the mosque (recited communally and individually), as a source of law, and as the foundation of Islamic education.

The Prophet Muhammad

The Prophet Muhammad is the second source of authority in Islam. His life provides the model (Sunnah) for how Muslims should live. Key events include: his birth c.570 CE in Makkah; the first revelation at age 40 in 610 CE; his mission in Makkah (610–622 CE) and the growing opposition he faced; the Hijrah (migration to Madinah in 622 CE), which marks year one of the Islamic calendar; his work in Madinah establishing the Muslim community; and his death in 632 CE.

Surah 48:26–29 praises the believers who accompanied the Prophet and describes the characteristics of his companions: firm against opponents, merciful to one another, performing prayer and seeking Allah’s approval. Surah 33:36–47 refers to the Prophet as the Seal of the Prophets and sets out his multiple roles: a witness, a bringer of good news and a warner. Muhammad’s significance today: Muslims follow his example in prayer, family life, business ethics and social conduct; his practice is recorded in the Hadith.

Ahl-ul-Bayt means “People of the House” — the Prophet’s household. Surah 33:32–34 addresses the Prophet’s household with specific instructions, which Shi’a Muslims interpret as confirming their special status and purity. For Shi’a Muslims, Caliph/Imam Ali and the Ahl-ul-Bayt are the rightful authorities after the Prophet. For Sunni Muslims, Ali is respected as the fourth of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, but not as a uniquely divinely appointed leader. This disagreement is the theological root of the Sunni–Shi’a split and continues to shape divergent approaches to religious authority.

The Hadith

The Hadith are the recorded sayings, actions and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad. They are the second major written source of Islamic guidance after the Qur’an. Each hadith has two parts: the isnad (the chain of transmitters going back to the Prophet) and the matn (the content or body of the report). Scholars assess a hadith’s authenticity by analysing the isnad: how trustworthy were the narrators? Were they contemporaries who could plausibly have witnessed the event?

Key Fact

The two most authoritative Sunni hadith collections are Sahih al-Bukhari (compiled by al-Bukhari, d.870 CE) and Sahih Muslim (compiled by Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj, d.875 CE). Shi’a Islam relies on its own hadith canon, known as the Four Books, which centre on reports from the Imams as well as the Prophet. This reflects the Shi’a conviction that the Imams are authoritative sources alongside the Prophet.

Shari’ah Law

Shari’ah Law is Islamic law derived from the Qur’an and Hadith, developed through scholarship. It governs worship, family life, business, criminal justice and social conduct. Two key legal tools are: qiyas (analogical reasoning, where a Qur’anic or hadith ruling is extended to a new situation by identifying a shared principle) and ijma (scholarly consensus). Surah 4:115 is a key Qur’anic reference: it warns against following a path other than “the path of the believers,” which scholars interpret as supporting the principle of ijma. Qadis (judges) and the ulema (scholars) are the trained experts who interpret and apply Shari’ah. Sunni Islam has four main legal schools (Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi’i, Hanbali); Shi’a Islam follows its own Ja’fari school, which gives greater weight to the Imams’ teachings.

The Imam in Shi’a Islam

In Shi’a Islam, the Imam is not simply a prayer leader but a divinely guided religious and political authority, believed to be sinless (ma’sum) and infallible in matters of faith. Nass is the doctrine that the designation of each Imam was divinely appointed and explicitly transmitted. The twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, is believed by Twelver Shi’a to have gone into occultation (divine hiding) and will return at the end of time. The Hadith of the pond of Khumm (Ghadir Khumm) is regarded by Shi’a Muslims as the Prophet’s explicit designation of Ali as the first Imam. In Sunni Islam, an imam is a prayer leader; the role carries no divine appointment or inerrancy. Sahih al-Bukhari 73:34–37 discusses the qualities expected of a Sunni imam — a role of learning and community service rather than divine authority.

Section 4: Forms of Expression and Ways of Life

Muslim Identity

Muslim identity is expressed through the shared ummah — the global community of believers. From birth, community ceremonies mark a child as part of the ummah (the Adhan whispered in the newborn’s ear; the Aqiqah ceremony). Expectations of modesty in dress and behaviour are rooted in Surah 24:30–31, which instructs both men and women to “lower their gaze and guard their private parts” and (for women) to “not display their adornments except to their husbands.” Interpretations of modest dress vary widely: some Muslim women wear a hijab (headscarf), niqab or abaya; others interpret modesty as a matter of character rather than specific dress.

Halal (permitted) and haram (forbidden) govern all areas of Muslim life: food (pork and blood are haram; meat must be slaughtered in the name of Allah), finance (riba, or interest/usury, is haram — Islamic banking uses profit-sharing instead), and conduct. These categories derive from the Qur’an and the Sunnah.

The Mosque

The mosque (masjid) is the centre of Muslim community life. Sahih al-Bukhari 2:39 describes the Prophet’s own mosque in Madinah and the practices associated with congregational prayer, establishing the template for mosque use. Key architectural features include: the mihrab (prayer niche indicating the direction of Makkah), the minbar (pulpit for Friday sermons), the minaret (tower for the call to prayer), and an area for wudu (ritual washing). In some mosques, a separate area is provided for women. The mosque is used for: daily and Friday (Jummah) prayer, Qur’an classes, community events and Eid celebrations.

Calligraphy

Calligraphy is one of the most important art forms in Islam. Islamic art avoids depicting human or animal figures in religious contexts because of concerns about idolatry — Surah 21:51–62 records Ibrahim destroying the idols of his people, establishing the Islamic rejection of images as objects of devotion. Calligraphy fulfils the artistic impulse while directing attention to Allah’s word rather than created beings. Qur’anic verses, the names of Allah and the Shahadah are rendered in intricate scripts. Calligraphy appears on mosque walls, in the Qur’an and in Islamic decorative art worldwide.

Sufism — The Mystical Tradition

Sufism is the mystical tradition within Islam. Sufis seek direct personal experience of Allah, emphasising inner purification, love of God and spiritual closeness over outward religious performance alone. Sufism is organised into brotherhoods (tariqas) led by spiritual teachers called shaykhs. Central practices include dhikr (remembrance — the rhythmic repetition of Allah’s names or Qur’anic phrases) and periods of extended fasting. Surah 13:28 is the key Qur’anic anchor: “Verily, in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest.”

Al-Ghazali (1058–1111 CE) was a Persian Islamic scholar, theologian and mystic. His most important work is the Ihya Ulum al-Din (Revival of the Religious Sciences) — a comprehensive guide to Islamic spirituality that integrates orthodox theology with Sufi practice. Al-Ghazali argued that Sufism was grounded in the Qur’an and the Sunnah, not in contradiction to them. He is credited with reconciling mysticism and orthodox scholarship within Sunni Islam. His Revival remains one of the most widely read works in Islamic literature.

Ibn al-Arabi (1165–1240 CE) was an Andalusian (Spanish-born) Sufi mystic and philosopher. He developed the influential and controversial concept of wahdat al-wujud (Unity of Being) — the idea that all existence is, in some sense, a reflection or manifestation of Allah’s being. This idea was contested by some orthodox scholars who felt it blurred the distinction between Creator and creation. Ibn al-Arabi wrote extensively on spiritual experience, the nature of prophecy and the inner dimensions of Islamic faith.

Rabi’a al-Adawiyya (c.714–801 CE) was a female Sufi saint from Basra (modern-day Iraq), one of the earliest and most celebrated figures in the Sufi tradition. She is especially known for her theology of pure love (mahabbah) for Allah — the idea that love for God should be free of any desire for paradise or fear of hell. Her poetry and teaching profoundly shaped the devotional dimension of Sufism. Rabi’a stands as a celebrated female figure in the Sufi tradition, reflecting Sufism’s relatively open approach to female spiritual authority.

Key Fact

The key Sufi figures to know are: al-Ghazali — Revival of the Religious Sciences; reconciled Sufism with orthodox Islam. Ibn al-Arabi — concept of Unity of Being (wahdat al-wujud). Rabi’a al-Adawiyya — pure love for Allah independent of reward or fear. Dhikr Qur’anic verse: Surah 13:28.

Muslim Charity

Beyond the obligatory Zakah (and Shi’a Khums), Muslims are encouraged to give sadaqah (voluntary charity). Surah 2:271–274 praises those who give in charity, especially those who give secretly: “If you give charity openly, it is good, but if you give it secretly to the poor, that is better for you.” One named Muslim charity is Islamic Relief Worldwide, which works to relieve poverty and suffering in the UK and globally. Muslim charities ground their work in the Qur’anic command to care for the poor, the orphan and the traveller — reflecting the Islamic understanding that wealth belongs ultimately to Allah and must be shared justly within the ummah.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sources of authority in Islam: Qur’an (Surah 53:4–18), Sunnah/Hadith (isnad and matn; Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim for Sunni; Four Books for Shi’a), Shari’ah Law (qiyas and ijma, anchored in Surah 4:115). The Imam is a divinely appointed sinless leader in Shi’a Islam (Nass, Hidden Imam); an imam is a community prayer leader in Sunni Islam.
  • Muslim identity: expressed through the ummah, modesty (Surah 24:30–31), halal/haram categories (including riba), mosque architecture (mihrab, minbar, minaret) and calligraphy as a rejection of idolatry (Surah 21:51–62).
  • Sufism: dhikr anchored in Surah 13:28. Three named teachers: al-Ghazali (Revival of the Religious Sciences), ibn al-Arabi (Unity of Being), Rabi’a al-Adawiyya (pure love for Allah). Sadaqah (voluntary charity, Surah 2:271–274) complements obligatory Zakah.

practice_questions.text: Outline three sources of authority used by Muslims to guide their faith and practice.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: the Qur'an (the direct word of Allah, Surah 53:4-18); the Sunnah/Hadith (the example and recorded sayings of the Prophet Muhammad, in collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari); Shari'ah Law (derived from Qur'an, Hadith, qiyas and ijma); the Imam (for Shi'a Muslims, a divinely appointed sinless leader). One mark per clearly distinct source.

practice_questions.text: Describe what Muslims believe about the role of the mosque in Muslim life.
practice_questions.model_answer: The mosque is the centre of Muslim community life, used for daily and Friday (Jummah) prayers, Qur'an classes and community events. Key features include the mihrab (prayer niche indicating Makkah), minbar (pulpit for Friday sermons) and minaret (tower for the call to prayer). Sahih al-Bukhari 2:39 connects the mosque to the Prophet's own practice in Madinah. Three clear points earn three marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Hadith is important for Muslims today.
practice_questions.model_answer: First way: The Hadith provides detailed guidance on how to practise Islamic duties that the Qur'an commands but does not specify in full. For example, the Qur'an commands Salah but the Hadith records the exact movements and words used by the Prophet. Without the Hadith, many aspects of Islamic worship and law would be impossible to perform correctly. Second way: The Hadith preserves the living example (Sunnah) of the Prophet Muhammad, who is described in the Qur'an as the best model for believers (Surah 33:21). By following the Hadith, Muslims ensure their practice is grounded in prophetic example, not personal interpretation. Two developed points, two marks each.

practice_questions.text:
Explain two reasons why calligraphy is important in Islam.
In your answer you must refer to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.model_answer: First reason: Calligraphy expresses devotion to Allah through the beauty of His word. Qur'anic verses and the names of Allah rendered in intricate script direct the viewer's attention to the divine, not to human or animal forms. Second reason: Calligraphy reflects Islam's rejection of idolatry. Surah 21:51-62 records Ibrahim destroying the idols of his people — establishing the Islamic conviction that images of created beings should not be made objects of veneration. By using calligraphy instead of figurative art in religious settings, Muslims honour Allah while avoiding anything that might lead to idol worship. The fifth mark requires Surah 21:51-62 as the named anchor.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the statement: 'Sufism represents the truest and most complete form of Islam.'
In your answer you should give developed arguments in support of and against this statement, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.model_answer: Arguments in support: Sufism seeks the inward, spiritual heart of Islamic practice — the direct experience of Allah that makes outward religious duties meaningful. Al-Ghazali, in his Revival of the Religious Sciences, argued that Sufism was not in tension with orthodox Islam but was its deepest fulfilment. Sufis emphasise Surah 13:28 — 'in the remembrance of Allah do hearts find rest' — as the goal of all religious practice. Rabi'a al-Adawiyya taught that love of Allah, free from any desire for reward, is the purest form of faith. Without this inward dimension, Sufis argue, religious practice risks becoming empty ritual. Arguments against: Many mainstream Sunni and Shi'a scholars have questioned aspects of Sufism. Ibn al-Arabi's concept of the Unity of Being (wahdat al-wujud) has been criticised as blurring the distinction between Allah and creation, which some scholars regard as incompatible with Tawhid. Some Muslim communities have rejected Sufi practices (music, dance, veneration of saints) on the grounds that they introduce innovations (bid'ah) not supported by the Qur'an or Hadith. From this perspective, the Qur'an and Sunnah — not mystical experience — are the authoritative guides to correct Islamic practice. Conclusion: A justified conclusion might note that Sufism has a long and respected history within mainstream Islam, including the endorsement of al-Ghazali, who was himself a respected orthodox scholar. However, describing it as the 'truest' form is contested — other Muslims regard strict adherence to the Qur'an and Sunnah without mystical additions as equally or more authentic. The statement overstates Sufism's claim by suggesting it supersedes other forms of Islamic practice. Mastering (10-12): both sides developed with named sources (al-Ghazali, Surah 13:28, ibn al-Arabi); weighing explicit; justified conclusion. Secure (7-9): both sides; one source; conclusion. Developing (4-6): one side dominant. Emerging (1-3): brief.

practice_questions.text: Outline three ways in which Shari'ah Law is developed and applied in Islam.
practice_questions.model_answer: Three from: it is derived from the Qur'an (the primary source); it draws on the Hadith (the Prophet's example); qiyas (analogical reasoning) extends Qur'anic rulings to new situations; ijma (scholarly consensus) establishes accepted rulings, supported by Surah 4:115; qadis (judges) and the ulema (scholars) apply and interpret the law. One mark per clearly distinct point.

glossary_terms.definition: Islamic law derived from the Qur'an, Hadith, scholarly consensus (ijma) and analogical reasoning (qiyas), governing all aspects of Muslim life.
The chain of transmission in a hadith — the list of narrators going back to the Prophet, used to assess the hadith's reliability.
The content or body of a hadith — the actual words or description of the Prophet's action, as distinct from the chain of narrators.
Analogical reasoning in Islamic jurisprudence — extending a Qur'anic or hadith ruling to a new situation by identifying a shared principle.
Scholarly consensus in Islamic jurisprudence — the agreement of qualified scholars on a legal ruling, supported by Surah 4:115.
The mystical dimension of Islam, emphasising direct personal experience of Allah through inner purification and practices such as dhikr.
Remembrance of Allah — a Sufi practice of rhythmic repetition of Allah's names or Qur'anic phrases. Anchored in Surah 13:28.
Voluntary charity in Islam, given freely for the sake of Allah beyond the obligatory Zakah. Praised in Surah 2:271-274.
The Shi'a doctrine that each Imam is divinely designated and explicitly appointed by the previous Imam or by the Prophet.
Lawful or permitted in Islam — the category of things, actions, food and drink that Muslims are allowed.
Forbidden or prohibited in Islam — the category of things, actions, food and drink that Muslims are not permitted.
Usury or interest in Islamic finance — charging or receiving interest on loans, which is prohibited in Islam as exploitative.
The household of the Prophet Muhammad. In Shi'a Islam, the Ahl-ul-Bayt are regarded as the divinely chosen leaders of the Muslim community.
